title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed p. 846 (Night 190, continuing nights-189), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 190 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. King Shahramān, calling on God's protection over his son's wits, denies all knowledge of the girl the prince says was sent to him and taken away before morning. He asks whether it was a jumble of dreams or fancies bred of food, since the boy went to sleep with his mind full of marriage; he curses marriage, its hour and whoever advised it, and tells him a lovely girl embracing him in his sleep was only a dream he took for waking. Qamar al-Zamān will not have it and makes his father swear; the king swears by God, the God of Moses and Abraham, that he knows nothing of her. The prince offers to give him an example that will show it happened while he was awake, and dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْمُوفِيَةُ لِلتِّسْعِينَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-mūfiyatu li-al-tisʿīna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the completing-one for-the-ninety after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and ninetieth night,
sentences.n: A round number takes a different turn of phrase: al-mūfiya li-al-tisʿīna, “the one that makes up the ninety”, from awfā, Form IV, “to bring to the full count”; li- marks the number completed. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْمَلِكَ شَهْرَمَانَ قَالَ لِوَلَدِهِ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ اسْمُ اللَّهِ حَوَالَيْكَ يَا وَلَدِي سَلَامَةُ عَقْلِكَ مِنَ الْجُنُونِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malika Shahramāna qāla li-waladihi Qamari al-Zamāni ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka yā waladī salāmatu ʿaqlika mina al-junūni
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-King Shahramān said to-his-son Qamar al-Zamān: (The) name (of) God (be) around-you, O my-son! (The) safety (of) your-mind from the-madness!
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that King Shahramān said to his son Qamar al-Zamān, “God’s name be about you, my son! May your mind be kept safe from madness!
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story with the words that ended the last night: ismu Allāhi ḥawālayka, “the name of God be round about you”, the protective formula said over one who seems touched, and salāmatu ʿaqlika mina al-junūni, a wish in the nominative with its predicate left unsaid. Here the king calls his son yā waladī, “my son”, where at the end of the last night he said yā wālidī. Qamari al-Zamāni stands in apposition to waladihi and so is genitive.

sentences.t: فَأَيُّ شَيْءٍ هٰذِهِ الصَّبِيَّةُ الَّتِي تَزْعُمُ أَنِّي أَرْسَلْتُهَا إِلَيْكَ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ ثُمَّ أَرْسَلْتُ آخُذُهَا مِنْ عِنْدِكَ قَبْلَ الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: fa-ayyu shayʾin hādhihi al-ṣabiyyatu allatī tazʿumu annī arsaltuhā ilayka fī hādhihi al-laylati thumma arsaltu ākhudhuhā min ʿindika qabla al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: So-what thing (is) this the-girl who you-claim that-I sent-her to-you in this the-night, then I-sent, I-take-her from with-you before the-morning?
sentences.i: What is this girl you claim I sent to you tonight, and then sent to take her away from you before morning?
sentences.n: fa-ayyu shayʾin, “what kind of thing”, a common way of asking “what is this?” with a note of disbelief; the shadda of فايّ is printed. zaʿama, “to claim”, often of a claim the speaker doubts. arsaltu ākhudhuhā, “I sent, I take her”: the second verb follows the first with no link, an imperfect of purpose or accompanying action, “I sent to take her”, where Classical prose would more often write li-ākhudhahā. The king repeats his son’s own story back to him. The ā of آخذها is printed with its madda.

sentences.t: فَوَاللَّهِ يَا وَلَدِي لَيْسَ لِي عِلْمٌ بِهٰذَا الْأَمْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-wa-Allāhi yā waladī laysa lī ʿilmun bi-hādhā al-amri
sentences.l: For-by-God, O my-son, there-is-not to-me knowledge of-this the-matter.
sentences.i: By God, my son, I know nothing of this matter.
sentences.n: wa-Allāhi, “by God”, the oath with wa- governing the genitive. laysa lī ʿilmun bi-, “I have no knowledge of”: li- of possession, and ʿilm takes its object with bi-.

sentences.t: فَبِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تُخْبِرَنِي هَلْ ذٰلِكَ أَضْغَاثُ أَحْلَامٍ أَوْ تَخَيُّلَاتُ طَعَامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-bi-Allāhi ʿalayka an tukhbiranī hal dhālika aḍghāthu aḥlāmin aw takhayyulātu ṭaʿāmin
sentences.l: So-by-God (I-adjure)-upon-you that you-tell-me: is that jumbles (of) dreams or fancies (of) food?
sentences.i: I adjure you by God, tell me: was that a jumble of dreams, or fancies bred of something you ate?
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God (I lay it) upon you”, the formula of earnest entreaty, with the verb of adjuring left out; an tukhbiranī, “that you tell me”, is what is asked. aḍghāthu aḥlāmin, “jumbled dreams”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (Sūrat Yūsuf 12:44), where the king of Egypt’s counsellors dismiss his dream of the seven cows; a ḍighth is properly a handful of mixed herbs or stalks. takhayyulātu ṭaʿāmin, “fancies of food”, is the other old explanation of a bad dream: the vapours of a heavy meal.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّكَ بِتَّ فِي هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَأَنْتَ مَشْغُولُ الْخَاطِرِ بِالزَّوَاجِ وَمُوَسْوِسٌ بِذِكْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-innaka bitta fī hādhihi al-laylati wa-anta mashghūlu al-khāṭiri bi-al-zawāji wa-muwaswisun bi-dhikrihi
sentences.l: For-indeed-you passed-the-night in this the-night while-you (were) occupied (of) the-mind with-the-marriage, and-obsessed with-(the)-mention-of-it.
sentences.i: For you spent this night with your mind taken up with marriage and haunted by the thought of it.
sentences.n: bāta, “to pass the night”; bitta, with the shadda printed, is its perfect 2ms, the doubled t of bit-ta. wa-anta …, “while you were …”, a clause of state. mashghūlu al-khāṭiri, “occupied of mind”: a participle in construct with the part it describes. muwaswis, “prey to waswasa”, the whispering of obsessive thoughts; the old lexicographers prefer the active form for the man so afflicted, and it is vocalised so here. bi- in both phrases marks what fills the mind.

sentences.t: فَلَعَنَ اللَّهُ الزَّوَاجَ وَسَاعَتَهُ وَلَعَنَ مَنْ أَشَارَبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-laʿana Allāhu al-zawāja wa-sāʿatahu wa-laʿana man ashāra bihi
sentences.l: So-cursed God the-marriage and-its-hour, and-cursed whoever advised-it.
sentences.i: God curse marriage and the hour of it, and curse whoever advised it!
sentences.n: A perfect used as a wish: laʿana Allāhu, “may God curse”. ashāra bi-, “to advise, recommend (something)”: bi- marks what is urged. The curse falls in effect on the vizier, who advised the king to marry his son and whom he has just blamed for the boy’s madness. The print runs اشار and به together, اشاربه; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: وَلَا شَكَّ وَلَا رَيْبَ أَنَّكَ مُتَكَدِّرُ الْمِزَاجِ مِنْ جِهَةِ الزَّوَاجِ
sentences.tr: wa-lā shakka wa-lā rayba annaka mutakaddiru al-mizāji min jihati al-zawāji
sentences.l: And-no doubt and-no uncertainty that-you (are) troubled (of) the-temper from (the) direction (of) the-marriage.
sentences.i: There is no doubt or question that your humour has been troubled over this business of marriage.
sentences.n: lā shakka wa-lā rayba, “no doubt and no uncertainty”, a doubled denial with the nouns in the accusative without tanwīn after lā of absolute negation; the shadda of شكّ is printed. mutakaddir, Form V participle of kadira, “to be muddied”, of water and so of mood; its shadda is printed. mizāj, “temperament”, the old medical word for one’s mixture of humours. min jihati, “on the side of, as regards”, a later prose idiom.

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتَ فِى الْمَنَامِ أَنَّ صَبِيَّةً مَلِيحَةً تُعَانِقُكَ وَأَنْتَ تَعْتَقِدُ فِي نَفْسِكَ أَنَّكَ رَأَيْتَهَا فِى الْيَقْظَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾayta fī al-manāmi anna ṣabiyyatan malīḥatan tuʿāniquka wa-anta taʿtaqidu fī nafsika annaka raʾaytahā fī al-yaqẓati
sentences.l: So-you-saw in the-sleep that a-girl comely (was) embracing-you, and-you believe in yourself that-you saw-her in the-waking.
sentences.i: So you saw in your sleep a lovely girl embracing you, and now you believe in your heart that you saw her awake.
sentences.n: The print has تعتقل, a misprint for تعتقد, corrected here. iʿtaqada, Form VIII, “to believe firmly”; fī nafsika, “in yourself”. The fatḥa on the tāʾ of فرأيتَ is printed, and so are the shadda of صبيّة and the hamza of رأيتها. The print writes في both ways in one line, فى and في. manām, “sleep”, and yaqẓa, “waking”, are the pair the whole dispute turns on.

sentences.t: وَهٰذَا كُلُّهُ يَا وَلَدِي أَضْغَاثُ أَحْلَامٍ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā kulluhu yā waladī aḍghāthu aḥlāmin
sentences.l: And-this, all-of-it, O my-son, (is) jumbles (of) dreams.
sentences.i: All this, my son, is a jumble of dreams.”
sentences.n: The shadda of كلّه is printed. The king comes back to the Qurʾānic phrase as his verdict.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ دَعْ عَنْكَ هٰذَا الْكَلَامَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Qamaru al-Zamāni daʿ ʿanka hādhā al-kalāma
sentences.l: So-said to-him Qamar al-Zamān: Leave from-you this the-talk,
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to him, “Leave this talk aside,
sentences.n: daʿ, imperative of wadaʿa, “let be”, a verb whose perfect is hardly used, taraka serving instead; daʿ ʿanka, “put away from you”.

sentences.t: وَاحْلِفْ لِي بِاللَّهِ الْخَالِقِ الْعَلَّامِ قَاصِمِ الْجَبَابِرَةِ وَمُبِيدِ الْأَ كَاسِرَةِ أَنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ عِنْدَكَ خَبَرٌ بِالصَّبِيَّةِ وَمَحَلِّهَا
sentences.tr: wa-iḥlif lī bi-Allāhi al-khāliqi al-ʿallāmi qāṣimi al-jabābirati wa-mubīdi al-akāsirati annahu lam yakun ʿindaka khabarun bi-al-ṣabiyyati wa-maḥallihā
sentences.l: and-swear to-me by-God, the-Creator, the-All-Knowing, (the) breaker (of) the-tyrants and-(the)-destroyer (of) the-Chosroeses, that-it not was with-you news of-the-girl and-her-place.
sentences.i: and swear to me by God the Creator, the All-Knowing, breaker of tyrants and destroyer of the Chosroes kings, that you had no word of the girl or of where she is.
sentences.n: ḥalafa bi-, “to swear by”: bi- marks what is sworn by; li-, “to me”, the one sworn to. The titles of God rhyme in pairs with what went before: al-kalām, al-ʿallām; al-jabābira, al-akāsira. al-ʿallām, intensive “the All-Knowing”; its shadda is printed. al-akāsira, plural of Kisrā, Chosroes, the Sasanian kings of Persia, the stock type of proud monarchs God has brought down. The print splits the word, الا كاسرة; the spacing is kept. annahu, “that it (is so that)”, the pronoun of the matter. khabar bi-, “knowledge of”. maḥall, “place, whereabouts”; its shadda, and that of بالصبيّة, are printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْمَلِكُ وَحَقِّ اللَّهِ الْعَظِيمِ إِلَٰهِ مُوسَى وَإِبْرَاهِيمَ إِنَّهُ لَمْ يَكُنْ لِي عِلْمٌ بِذٰلِكَ وَلَاعِنْدِي مِنْهُ خَبَرٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-maliku wa-ḥaqqi Allāhi al-ʿaẓīmi ilāhi Mūsā wa-Ibrāhīma innahu lam yakun lī ʿilmun bi-dhālika wa-lā ʿindī minhu khabarun
sentences.l: So-said to-him the-king: By-(the)-right (of) God the-Mighty, (the) God (of) Moses and-Abraham, indeed-it not was to-me knowledge of-that, nor with-me of-it news.
sentences.i: The king said to him, “By the truth of God the Almighty, God of Moses and Abraham, I knew nothing of it and have had no word of it.
sentences.n: wa-ḥaqqi Allāhi, “by the right of God”, an oath with wa- governing the genitive. The oath’s answer is introduced by inna, so innahu here, where the son’s “swear that” took annahu. The print sets a fatḥa on the lām of الَه, marking it as ilāh, “god”, not the particle illā; the long ā is supplied with a dagger alif. Ibrāhīm, a foreign name, takes no tanwīn and has -a in the genitive. The print runs ولا and عندي together, ولاعندي; the spacing is kept. minhu khabarun, “news of it”: min of the source.

sentences.t: وَإِنَّمَا ذٰلِكَ أَضْغَاثُ أَحْلَامٍ رَأَيْتَهُ أَنْتَ فِى الْمَنَامِ
sentences.tr: wa-innamā dhālika aḍghāthu aḥlāmin raʾaytahu anta fī al-manāmi
sentences.l: And-only that (is) jumbles (of) dreams (which) you-saw-it, you, in the-sleep.
sentences.i: It is only a jumble of dreams that you saw in your sleep.”
sentences.n: innamā, “only, it is nothing but”. raʾaytahu, “you saw it”, an unmarked relative clause after an indefinite; anta adds emphasis, “you yourself”. The hamza of رأيته is printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ لِوَالِدِهِ أَنَا أَضْرِبُ لَكَ مَثَلًا يُبَيِّنُ لَكَ أَنَّ هٰذَا كَانَ فِى الْيَقْظَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla Qamaru al-Zamāni li-wālidihi anā aḍribu laka mathalan yubayyinu laka anna hādhā kāna fī al-yaqẓati
sentences.l: So-said Qamar al-Zamān to-his-father: I, I-strike for-you a-likeness (that) makes-clear to-you that this was in the-waking.
sentences.i: Qamar al-Zamān said to his father, “I will give you an example that will show you this happened when I was awake.”
sentences.n: ḍaraba mathalan, “to strike a likeness”, that is, to give an example or parable, a Qurʾānic idiom; laka, “for you”. yubayyinu, Form II, “to make plain”, an unmarked relative clause after mathalan; its shadda is printed.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The print has البصاح, a misprint for الصباح, corrected here. The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
